title: Cyclotomic Arithmetic and Reciprocity via Frobenius

items.title: Cyclotomic conductor of a full cyclotomic field
items.statement: For K=Q(ζ_n), its cyclotomic conductor is the least positive f for which K is contained in Q(ζ_f). This is only a conductor of a full cyclotomic field, not an Artin conductor or a conductor assigned to an arbitrary abelian field.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.strategy: The set of admissible f contains n; the least exists by well-ordering. Do not infer that a general abelian field lies in a cyclotomic field. The later conductor theorem computes f and proves the reduced-index convention.

items.title: Prime-power cyclotomic ring, discriminant support and p factor
items.statement: For a prime p and a≥1, put K=Q(ζ_{p^a}), e=φ(p^a), λ=1−ζ_{p^a}. Then O_K=Z[ζ_{p^a}], (p)=(λ)^e, the power basis is integral, and the discriminant of this basis is a signed power of p with absolute value p^{p^{a−1}(a(p−1)−1)}.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: Use Φ_{p^a}(1)=p and that (1−ζ^u)/(1−ζ) and its inverse lie in Z[ζ] for p∤u to get p=unit·λ^e. Differentiate Φ_{p^a}(X)(X^{p^{a−1}}−1)=X^{p^a}−1 at ζ; norm of 1−ζ^{p^{a−1}} is p^{p^{a−1}}, giving the displayed discriminant exponent. The order-index formula confines [O_K:Z[ζ]] to a p-power. Show Z∩λO_K=pZ using λ^e=p·unit and O_K∩Q=Z. Expanding x∈pO_K∩Z[ζ] in the λ-power basis, successively reduce its coefficients modulo λ to show each divisible by p. Thus O_K∩p^{-1}Z[ζ]=Z[ζ]; iterate to kill the whole p-power index. The p=2,a=1 degree-one case follows with λ=2 and exponent zero.

items.title: Integral basis and discriminant of a coprime-discriminant compositum
items.statement: Suppose K,L are number fields with [KL:Q]=[K:Q][L:Q], given integral bases, and gcd(d_K,d_L)=1. Then O_{KL}=O_K O_L; products of the two bases form an integral basis, and d_{KL}=d_K^{[L:Q]}d_L^{[K:Q]}.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: Use degree multiplication and Q-basis structure constants to show the spans of the α_i over L and the β_j over K are finite-dimensional subalgebras of KL, then fields via injective and surjective multiplication maps, hence bases. The trace matrix gives a common denominator r with r|d_K a_ij and, symmetrically, r|d_L a_ij; the reduced-denominator Bezout identity yields r|d_K and r|d_L. For the discriminant, factor the embedding matrix and calculate the two determinants using separate valid index orderings.

items.title: Ring of integers of every cyclotomic field
items.statement: For every n≥1, O_{Q(ζ_n)}=Z[ζ_n], and 1,ζ_n,…,ζ_n^{φ(n)−1} is an integral basis.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: For n=1 use O_Q=Z with basis 1. Factor n into pairwise coprime prime powers. Their fields have product degree φ(n) by irreducibility and totient multiplicativity; the compositum is Q(ζ_n). The prime-power lemma gives each ring and discriminant support at its own prime. Repeatedly apply the coprime-discriminant compositum lemma, retaining the signed discriminant product and integral basis. Bezout exponents for coprime levels show Z[ζ_{p^a},ζ_m]=Z[ζ_{p^a m}]. Irreducibility of Φ_n then makes 1,ζ_n,…,ζ_n^{φ(n)−1} a basis. After the later conductor theorem proves the least containing level is a displayed reduced index f for K, this result applies at n=f; no conductor equality is presumed here.

items.title: Signed discriminant of a cyclotomic field
items.statement: For a reduced index f>1 (f odd or 4|f) and K=Q(ζ_f), the signed field discriminant is d_K=(−1)^{φ(f)/2} f^{φ(f)}/∏_{p|f}p^{φ(f)/(p−1)}. For f=1, d_Q=1. The conductor theorem later identifies f as the intrinsic conductor.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: For each reduced f>1, combine the prime-power absolute discriminants via the coprime-discriminant compositum formula and obtain the sign from complex conjugate embedding pairs. Treat f=1 separately: the integral basis (1) of Q has trace Gram matrix [1], hence discriminant 1 by the discriminant definition. Do not evaluate the sign formula at f=1.

items.title: Total ramification at a prime-power cyclotomic level
items.statement: For a≥1 and K=Q(ζ_{p^a}), pO_K=(1−ζ_{p^a})^{φ(p^a)}. The principal ideal (1−ζ_{p^a}) is the unique prime above p and has residue field F_p.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: The prime-power lemma gives the ideal equality. Quotient Z[ζ]/(1−ζ) is Z/(Φ_{p^a}(1))=F_p, so the displayed ideal is prime. Every prime over p contains its e-th power and therefore contains (1−ζ); uniqueness and residue degree one follow. For p^a=2, e=1 and K=Q, so the same statement holds.

items.title: Choice-free prime factorisation for a monogenic number ring
items.statement: Let K=Q(α) be a number field with O_K=Z[α], and let F be the monic minimal polynomial of α. For a rational prime p, factor F mod p as ∏_i g_i^{a_i} into distinct monic irreducibles. Then pO_K=∏_i P_i^{a_i}, where P_i=(p,g_i(α)) are distinct primes with residue degrees deg g_i. This finite argument uses no Axiom of Choice.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Theorem 3.41 and proof, pp.62–63

items.proof_strategy: Use A/pA ≅ F_p[t]/(F̄) and polynomial CRT to identify the distinct primes P_i and residue degrees. Apply the published choice-free integral ideal factorisation to write pA=∏Q_i^{e_i}; its local proof supplies the DVR nilpotency-index and one-dimensional layer calculations. Localize at each P_i, identify A_{P_i}/p with F_p[t]_(g_i)/(g_i^{a_i}), and compare exact nilpotency indices to get e_i=a_i. Retain repeated factors; no choices are made.

items.title: Arithmetic Frobenius is the power map in an unramified cyclotomic field
items.statement: For a reduced index f and a rational prime ℓ∤f, the unique arithmetic Frobenius in Q(ζ_f)/Q is σ_ℓ: ζ_f↦ζ_f^ℓ, independent of the prime above ℓ because the Galois group is abelian.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: Squarefree finite-field cyclotomic factorization and the monogenic lemma show ℓ is unramified. At each prime P, arithmetic Frobenius satisfies the ℓ-power congruence on ζ. Embed the residue field into a splitting field of t^f−1 to show the reduced ζ has exact order f. Writing Frob=σ_b and comparing powers directly gives b≡ℓ mod f, without applying σ_ℓ^{-1} modulo P before stability is known. Handle f=1 separately.

items.title: Prime factorisation in a cyclotomic field
items.statement: Let f≥1 be a reduced index (f odd or 4|f), write f=ℓ^a m with (ℓ,m)=1, and put e=φ(ℓ^a), d=ord_m(ℓ), g=φ(m)/d, with φ(1)=ord_1(ℓ)=1. Then ℓO_{Q(ζ_f)}=(P_1···P_g)^e with distinct primes P_i of residue degree d, and edg=φ(f).

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: Use O_K/ℓO_K=F_ℓ[X]/(Φ_f mod ℓ). If a=0, the finite-field cyclotomic factor theorem gives g distinct irreducible factors, each degree d. If a≥1, Φ_{ℓ^a m}(X)=Φ_m(X^{ℓ^a})/Φ_m(X^{ℓ^{a−1}}) reduces to Φ_m(X)^{φ(ℓ^a)}, because ℓ∤m; factor Φ_m as before. Apply the preceding local monogenic factorisation lemma to convert the exact polynomial multiplicities to prime-ideal exponents e, with residue fields of degree d. In the ℓ-power factor this matches the total-ramification corollary; when a=0 the power map is arithmetic Frobenius and its orbit length is d. The m=1 and f=1 cases use the explicit order-one conventions. This avoids the published general ZF-factorisation theorem and its transitive Choice path.

items.title: Ramification primes of a reduced cyclotomic conductor
items.statement: A rational prime ℓ ramifies in Q(ζ_f) if and only if ℓ divides its reduced index f.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: The factorisation theorem gives e=φ(ℓ^a). If ℓ∤f, a=0 and e=1. If ℓ|f with f reduced, either ℓ is odd and a≥1 or ℓ=2 and a≥2; in both cases e>1. An unreduced displayed index such as 6 is deliberately excluded.

items.title: Conductor of a full cyclotomic field
items.statement: The conductor of Q(ζ_n) is n except when n≡2 mod 4, in which case it is n/2. In particular Q(ζ_{2m})=Q(ζ_m) for odd m and Q(ζ_2)=Q has conductor 1.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: Reduce each index to t(N), which preserves the full cyclotomic field. For an admissible g, put r=t(n), s=t(g), and obtain Q(zeta_r)⊆Q(zeta_s). For each p|r, choose a prime Q above p in the upper field using its prime factorisation, and contract it to P=Q∩O_lower; inverse-image primality, p∈P, and P∩Z=(p) prove that P is a nonzero prime above p. The inertia tower then shows φ(p^{v_p(r)}) divides φ(p^{v_p(s)}); reduced-index monotonicity gives r|s≤g and proves leastness.

items.title: Decomposition of an unramified prime in a cyclotomic field
items.statement: For a rational prime ℓ not dividing the conductor f of K=Q(ζ_f), every prime over ℓ has residue degree ord_f(ℓ), and there are φ(f)/ord_f(ℓ) such primes.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: Apply the factorisation theorem with a=0, m=f and e=1. The resulting d equals the order of σ_ℓ=Frob_ℓ under the cyclotomic Galois identification, so the number of factors is φ(f)/d. For f=1 use ord_1(ℓ)=1.

items.title: Complete splitting criterion for a cyclotomic field
items.statement: For ℓ not dividing the conductor f, ℓ splits completely in Q(ζ_f) if and only if ℓ≡1 mod f.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: The preceding unramified decomposition formula gives residue degree ord_f(ℓ) and number φ(f)/ord_f(ℓ). Complete splitting means precisely φ(f) distinct degree-one primes, so it is equivalent to ord_f(ℓ)=1, that is ℓ≡1 mod f. The arithmetic Frobenius lemma identifies the same condition with trivial σ_ℓ. The f=1 case is tautological; no generic splitting theorem is needed.

items.title: Quadratic Gauss sum in a prime cyclotomic field
items.statement: For an odd prime p and a fixed primitive pth root ζ_p, τ_p=Σ_{a mod p}(a/p)ζ_p^a in Z[ζ_p]; the zero term vanishes. The chosen root is part of the data.

references.title: Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3
J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19

items.strategy: This finite sum is an algebraic integer because every summand is in Z[ζ_p]. Fix the primitive root explicitly; changing it can change the sign of τ_p, but not the square or generated quadratic field.

items.title: Galois action on the quadratic Gauss sum
items.statement: For b a nonzero class modulo an odd prime p and σ_b(ζ_p)=ζ_p^b, one has σ_b(τ_p)=(b/p)τ_p.

references.title: Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3
J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19

items.proof_strategy: Apply σ_b termwise and substitute c=ba in the finite sum. The coefficient becomes (b^{-1}c/p)=(b/p)(c/p), because the Legendre symbol is multiplicative and (b/p)^2=1. The zero term stays zero; no analytic Gauss-sum sign is used.

items.title: Square of the quadratic Gauss sum
items.statement: For odd prime p, τ_p²=p*=(−1)^{(p−1)/2}p.

references.title: Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3
J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19

items.proof_strategy: Write τ²=Σ_{s≠0,u}(s/p)(su/p)ζ^{s(1+u)}=Σ_u(u/p)Σ_{s≠0}ζ^{s(1+u)}. The inner sum is p−1 for u=−1 and −1 otherwise; Σ_u(u/p)=0 by pairing a nonsquare with squares. Therefore τ²=p(−1/p)=p*. The proof uses only finite sums and the already proved first supplement, not quadratic reciprocity or an analytic sign choice.

items.title: Quadratic subfield generated by the Gauss sum
items.statement: For odd prime p, the unique degree-two intermediate field of Q(ζ_p)/Q is Q(τ_p)=Q(√p*). At p=3 it may equal the full cyclotomic field.

references.title: Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3
J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19

items.proof_strategy: The square formula makes τ nonzero and τ²=p* a nonsquare rational integer, so Q(τ) has degree two. The action lemma shows that exactly the square classes fix τ, giving the index-two subgroup. The published uniqueness theorem then identifies the field. Since τ²=p*, choice of the primitive root changes only τ by a Legendre sign, never its square or field.

items.title: Quadratic reciprocity as a Frobenius restriction identity
items.statement: For distinct odd primes p,q, arithmetic Frob_q in Q(ζ_p) sends ζ_p to ζ_p^q and τ_p to (q/p)τ_p. Its restriction to Q(√p*) acts by (p*/q) on τ_p. Hence (p*/q)=(q/p).

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24
Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3

items.proof_strategy: For odd q≠p, the local cyclotomic Frobenius lemma gives σ_q(ζ)=ζ^q and σ_q(x)≡x^q modulo every prime over q. The Gauss action lemma yields σ_q(τ)=(q/p)τ. Since τ²=p*, one also has τ^q=τ(p*)^{(q−1)/2}≡(p*/q)τ by Euler’s criterion. The image of τ modulo a prime above q is nonzero because q∤p*: otherwise τ²=p* would vanish there. Both signs are ±1 and q is odd, so reduction distinguishes them; equality of the two residues forces (p*/q)=(q/p). This directly proves the restriction action on Q(τ)=Q(√p*) and avoids the generic tower theorem. No earlier quadratic-reciprocity result or geometric Frobenius is used.

items.title: Quadratic reciprocity via Frobenius
items.statement: For distinct odd primes p,q, (p/q)(q/p)=(−1)^{(p−1)(q−1)/4}.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3

items.proof_strategy: Expand p*=(−1)^{(p−1)/2}p in (p*/q)=(q/p); multiply by (p/q) and use multiplicativity and the first supplement at q. The exponent is ((p−1)/2)((q−1)/2). The earlier published quadratic reciprocity theorem is not used as a supplier.

items.title: First supplement from Frobenius on Q(i)
items.statement: For odd q, arithmetic Frob_q on Q(i)=Q(ζ_4) sends i to (−1)^{(q−1)/2}i; this is the quadratic sign (−1/q).

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24
Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3

items.proof_strategy: The power-map lemma gives i↦i^q=(−1)^{(q−1)/2}i. In the quadratic field i²=−1, reduction modulo a prime over odd q and Euler’s criterion identify the same sign with (−1/q); i is nonzero modulo q. This recovers the supplement without depending on its earlier statement.

items.title: Second supplement from Frobenius on Q(ζ_8)
items.statement: For odd q, Q(√2) is a quadratic subfield of Q(ζ_8), and arithmetic Frobenius restricts to multiplication by (2/q)=(−1)^{(q²−1)/8} on √2.

references.title: Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3
J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19

items.proof_strategy: Set t=ζ_8+ζ_8^{-1}; t²=2. For q modulo 8 equal to 1 or 7, ζ_8^q+ζ_8^{-q}=t; for 3 or 5 it is −t. Thus Frob_q acts by the sign (−1)^{(q²−1)/8}. Since t²=2 and q is odd, reduction plus Euler’s criterion identifies this sign with (2/q); t remains nonzero modulo q. This is independent of the earlier second-supplement theorem.

title: Cyclotomic Arithmetic and Reciprocity via Frobenius — Examples

items.title: The reduced conductor of Q(ζ_6)
items.statement: Q(ζ_6)=Q(ζ_3), its conductor is 3, and the rational prime 2 is unramified.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: For ζ_3 of order 3, −ζ_3 has order 6, so the fields agree. The conductor theorem gives f=3; the ramification criterion then excludes 2. State why the unreduced display index 6 would give the wrong ramification inference.

items.title: Arithmetic of Q(ζ_5)
items.statement: For K=Q(ζ_5), O_K=Z[ζ_5], d_K=125; 5 is totally ramified, 2 is unramified with residue degree four and trivial inertia, and 11 splits completely.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: At f=5 the basis is 1,ζ,ζ²,ζ³ and d=5^4/5=125. The prime 5 has (5)=(1−ζ)^4 with residue F_5. Order of 2 mod 5 is four, so the unique prime over 2 has residue F_16 and e=1. Its inertia kernel is trivial directly: reduction of ζ has order 5 in F_16; if σ_b fixes every residue, it fixes the reduced ζ, so b≡1 mod5 and σ_b=1. Since 11≡1 mod5 it has four distinct degree-one primes.

items.title: Prime decomposition in Q(ζ_8)
items.statement: For K=Q(ζ_8), d_K=2^8; every odd prime has residue degree 1 if it is 1 mod 8 and degree 2 otherwise, with respectively four or two primes above it.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: The discriminant formula gives 8^4/2^4=2^8. Units modulo 8 are 1,3,5,7; the identity has order one and the other three classes have order two. Apply the decomposition formula and note all odd primes are unramified.

items.title: Prime decomposition in Q(ζ_12)
items.statement: For K=Q(ζ_12), d_K=144. The primes 2 and 3 each have a unique prime above them with e=f=2; any ℓ∤12 splits into four degree-one primes if ℓ≡1 mod12, and two degree-two primes for the classes 5,7,11 mod12.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Conrad–Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory, Chs. 10–12 and 24

items.proof_strategy: Compute 12^4/(2^4·3^2)=144. For ℓ=2, write 12=2²·3: e=φ(4)=2, d=ord_3(2)=2, g=1. For ℓ=3, write 12=3·4: e=2, d=ord_4(3)=2, g=1. The unit group modulo 12 has exponent two, with identity class 1; apply the unramified formula to the four residue classes.

items.title: Quadratic Gauss sum at p=3
items.statement: For the standard complex root ζ_3=e^{2πi/3}, τ_3=ζ_3−ζ_3²=i√3 and τ_3²=−3.

references.title: Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3
J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19

items.proof_strategy: The nonzero Legendre values are (1/3)=1 and (2/3)=−1. Substitute ζ_3=−1/2+i√3/2 and ζ_3² its conjugate, subtract, then square. Identify p*=−3 in the general theorem.

items.title: Quadratic Gauss sum at p=5
items.statement: For the standard root ζ_5=e^{2πi/5}, τ_5=√5; its Galois stabilizer is the square subgroup {1,4} of (Z/5Z)^×.

references.title: Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3
J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19

items.proof_strategy: The residue signs give τ=ζ+ζ⁴−ζ²−ζ³=1+2t with t=ζ+ζ⁴=2cos(2π/5)>0. From Φ_5(ζ)=0 derive t²+t−1=0, so t=(√5−1)/2 and τ=√5. The action lemma makes σ_b fix nonzero τ exactly when (b/5)=1, i.e. b=1,4.

items.title: Quadratic subfield of Q(ζ_7)
items.statement: The unique degree-two intermediate field of Q(ζ_7)/Q is Q(√−7).

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3

items.proof_strategy: Set p=7 in p*=(−1)^{(p−1)/2}p=−7 and apply the Gauss-sum subfield theorem; explain that the quadratic field is unique even though the Gauss-sum generator changes sign with a primitive-root change.

items.title: Frobenius restriction for p=5 and q=3
items.statement: In Q(ζ_5), arithmetic Frob_3 acts nontrivially on Q(√5): (3/5)=(5/3)=−1.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19
Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3

items.proof_strategy: The classes 3 mod5 and 5 mod3=2 are nonsquares. The power map ζ_5↦ζ_5³ sends τ_5 to −τ_5=−√5; the quadratic reduction description gives (5/3)=−1. Both are actions of the same arithmetic Frobenius restriction.

items.title: Second supplement in four residue classes modulo eight
items.statement: For q≡1,3,5,7 mod8, Frob_q on √2=ζ_8+ζ_8^{-1} has signs +,−,−,+ respectively, matching (2/q).

references.title: Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3
J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19

items.proof_strategy: Calculate ζ_8^q+ζ_8^{-q} for the four odd residue classes: q=1,7 preserves the sum; q=3,5 negates it. Evaluate parity of (q²−1)/8 in each class and compare the four signs.

items.title: The sign of a quadratic Gauss sum needs a chosen primitive root
items.statement: A quadratic Gauss sum has no canonical sign without its primitive-root or complex-embedding convention, even though τ_p² and Q(τ_p) are unchanged.

references.title: Jerry Shurman, Math 361 Ninth Lecture, §§2–3
J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. 6 and Ch. 8 Examples 8.18–8.19

items.proof_strategy: Take p=3, ζ=e^{2πi/3}, so τ=ζ−ζ²=i√3. Replacing the primitive root by ζ² (a nonsquare exponent) changes the finite sum to ζ²−ζ=−i√3 by the action lemma. Both squares are −3 and both generate Q(√−3), disproving a root-independent sign claim. This does not contradict the analytic sign theorem after fixing a standard complex embedding.
